evidence: Read spec/1.3.0.md §5 ('`done` — converged, or at the cap as in `tp review`') and §9 row 10 (fixture 'one round recorded holding a `high` finding', SHALL '`done: true, done_by: cap` and `--check` exits 0'). Read internal/engine/loopdone.go loopDone: at the cap it counts `Undisposed` (rows with no disposition) and `BlockingFixedAtCap`, and sets `Done, By = true, DoneByCap` only when both are 0. Round-1 finding #2 (review-round-1.ndjson) itself describes the verdict as 'a loop the cap ended with every latest finding dispositioned'.
finding: Row 10, rewritten to pin the cap-done verdict, contradicts the tp review cap rule §5 says it reuses. Its fixture is `review_max_rounds` 1 with one recorded round holding an undispositioned `high` finding, and it asserts `done: true, done_by: cap` and `--check` exit 0. In tp review a loop is done by cap only when every finding of the latest round carries a disposition and no blocking finding is marked fixed; an open high finding keeps `done: false` and `--check` at 1. The repair of the round-1 cap-done finding therefore pins the opposite of 'at the cap as in tp review': an implementation that ports tp review's verdict fails row 10, and one that passes row 10 lets Workflow E move past a slice whose high finding nobody answered.

evidence: spec/1.3.0.md §5: "The index lists every unit with a hash covering its own block and the blocks of its direct dependencies." §9 row 4 fixture: "`x → ui-rule-checker`, `screen` tagged `ui` with `screen → x`" (arrow = depends_on). §9 row 7: "one `why` on `a` is edited ... in round 3 exactly `a` and its dependant `b` un-carried" over "The chain is `a → b → c → d`".
finding: Row 7 cannot pass under §5's carry hash whichever way the chain's arrows are read. Row 4 fixes the arrow as `depends_on` (`x → ui-rule-checker`, `screen → x`, `screen` the dependent), so in the chain `a → b → c → d`, `a` depends on `b` and nothing depends on `a`. Editing a `why` on `a` changes only `a`'s own block. `b`'s hash covers `b`'s block and the blocks of `b`'s direct dependencies (`c`), so `b` stays carried. The row demands that `b` be un-carried as `a`'s dependant, which `b` is not. Read the other way (`b` depends on `a`), `a` has no outgoing edge and so no `why` to edit. The mutant ("hash the own block only, so `b` stays carried") then produces the same result as a correct implementation.
suggestion: Edit the `why` on `b`'s edge to `c` (or `a`'s title with the chain reversed) and name the true dependant, e.g. "exactly `b` and its dependant `a` un-carried".

evidence: spec/1.3.0.md §5 line 115-116: "The index lists every unit with a hash covering its own block and the blocks of its direct dependencies." vs §9 row 7 (line 200): "in round 3 exactly `a` and its dependant `b` un-carried" with mutant "hash the own block only, so `b` stays carried". Edge direction: row 4 (line 197) "`x → ui-rule-checker`, `screen` tagged `ui` with `screen → x`" (arrow = depends on); §5 line 111 "each outgoing edge with its `why`" puts `a → b`'s why in `a`'s block.
finding: Row 7's expected result contradicts §5's hash rule given the edge direction the rest of §9 uses. The arrow means 'depends on' (row 4: `x → ui-rule-checker` is the path to the provider; row 11: `d → a` closes a cycle with `a → b → c → d`). So in the chain `a` depends on `b`, `a` has no dependant, and `a`'s `why` sits in `a`'s own block. Under §5 the only hash covering `a`'s block is `a`'s own, because nothing depends on `a`. Editing that `why` therefore un-carries `a` alone. The row expects `a` and 'its dependant `b`' to be un-carried. That outcome is the one its own mutant ('hash the own block only, so `b` stays carried') is said to produce, so a correct implementation fails the row and the mutant cannot be told apart from it.
suggestion: Edit the `why` on `b` (edge `b → c`) or a field of `c`, and expect the edited unit plus the unit that depends on it to be un-carried (`b` only, or `c` and `b`). Or state that the arrow in 'the chain' means 'is depended on by'. Either way, check rows 6, 11 and 19 against the chosen direction.

evidence: spec/1.3.0.md §5: "`--status --check` exits 0 only when the slice's loop is `done` — converged, or at the cap as in `tp review`". skills/tp/SKILL.md:705: "The loop is **done** (`done_by: cap`) when every finding of the latest round carries a disposition in its recorded round file … A blocking finding marked `fixed` at the cap keeps the loop open (`blocking_fixed_at_cap`)". §9 row 10 fixture: "one round recorded holding a `high` finding" (no disposition), expecting "`done: true, done_by: cap` and `--check` exits 0".
finding: Row 10 expects `done: true, done_by: cap` and `--check` exit 0 from a capped round whose `high` finding has no disposition. That contradicts §5's 'at the cap as in `tp review`'. In tp review, a capped loop is done only once every finding of the latest round carries a disposition, and a blocking finding marked `fixed` at the cap keeps the loop open. An implementation that reuses tp review's cap verdict, as §5 says, reports `done: false` and exits 1 on this fixture, which is exactly the row's mutant ('keep `--check` at 1'). So the row fails the correct implementation and passes the mutant.
suggestion: Add the disposition to row 10's fixture (the `high` row resolved `wontfix` with evidence), and add the undispositioned case as a second assertion: `done: false` and `--check` exits 1.

evidence: spec/1.3.0.md §3: "a write whose after-state holds an error the before-state did not exits 1 naming the rule and writes nothing, so a file already holding an error is repaired one write at a time." §9 row 2: fixture "a file with a dangling edge on `a`; first `add` closes a cycle `b → a → b`, then `set` replaces `a`'s `depends_on` with a legal edge"; mutant "refuse any after-state error, so the repairing `set` exits 1". After the refused add, the set's after-state is error-free, so the mutant exits 0.
finding: Row 2's mutant ('refuse any after-state error') cannot go red against the row's fixture. The first `add` adds an error, so both readings refuse it and the file keeps only a's dangling edge. The repairing `set` then removes that error and adds none, so the after-state holds no error at all, and the mutant exits 0 exactly like the correct implementation. The behaviour §3 adds ('a write whose after-state holds an error the before-state did not') only differs from the mutant when an old error survives the write, and no step of the row leaves one standing. So the 'repaired one write at a time' rule has no row that can fail it.
suggestion: Start from a file holding two independent errors (say a dangling edge on `a` and an empty `why` on `c`). Have the `set` repair only one and expect exit 0 with the other still reported by `tp epic lint`. Or add a legal unrelated epic to the one-error file and expect exit 0. The mutant exits 1 in either case.

evidence: spec/1.3.0.md §3: "a write whose after-state holds an error the before-state did not exits 1 naming the rule"; §9 row 2 tests only a new rule (`cycle`) against an old one (`dangling-reference`), so neither reading is pinned.
finding: "an error the before-state did not [hold]" does not say whether an error is identified by rule slug or by finding instance. Two correct implementations disagree on a file that already holds a `dangling-reference` on `a` when a write adds a second dangling edge on `c`. Comparing by slug accepts the write, because the rule already fired, and writes a new defect. Comparing by instance refuses it. A finding's identity also needs defining for `cycle`, whose single finding changes its `epic`/`message` when a write extends an existing cycle.

evidence: spec/1.3.0.md §7: "interview the topic → `tp epic set milestones=…` on a new file → `tp epic add --bulk`". §4: "3 when there is no file". §3 names the writers but none creates the file. §9 row 20 fixture: "an empty file; tracks `[[A]]`".
finding: No writer is said to create the file, and Workflow E starts on 'a new file'. One implementation of `tp epic set milestones=…` creates `.tp/epics.json` when it is absent. Another refuses because there is no file, the case lint gives exit 3 for. Row 20's fixture is 'an empty file', which, as a zero-byte file, is not valid JSON and is neither state. So the row does not pin the first step of Workflow E.

evidence: Read spec/1.3.0.md §3 (delta rule, 'exits 1 naming the rule') and §4 (finding shape `{rule, severity, epic, message}`; 'A cycle is one finding, `epic` its first member in file order'). Rows 2 and 20 each exercise only one error, so neither row fixes the identity.
finding: The repair settled the delta reading ('an error the before-state did not' hold) without saying how two errors are compared, and that comparison is the new decision. If errors are compared by rule slug, a file that already holds one `dangling-reference` accepts any number of new dangling edges, and a file with one cycle accepts a second, unrelated cycle. If they are compared by finding (rule plus `epic`, or message), those writes are refused. A cycle's identity is also unstable: §4 sets its `epic` to the first member in file order, so a write that adds or reorders epics can change an existing cycle's finding without adding an error. Two implementations that both follow §3 disagree on whether a writer can make a broken file worse, which the write guard exists to prevent.

evidence: spec/1.3.0.md §3: "`tp epic remove` refuses an epic another epic depends on unless `--force`, which also drops the edges into it and its gate memberships; a provider named in `tag_checks` is refused even then." §9 rows 1-20: no row runs `tp epic remove` outside row 12's TP_UNATTENDED fence.
finding: `tp epic remove` makes three decisions, and no §9 row covers any of them. It refuses an epic another epic depends on unless `--force`. `--force` also drops the edges into the epic and its gate memberships. A `tag_checks` provider is refused even under `--force`. A remove that always deletes and leaves dangling edges would be refused only by the after-state lint, with a different refusal. One that ignores the provider fence under `--force`, or drops edges but leaves gate members, passes every row. Row 12 only checks that `remove` is fenced under TP_UNATTENDED.
suggestion: Add one row over the chain plus a gate and a `tag_checks` provider. Without `--force`, removing `c` exits 1 with the file byte-identical. With `--force`, the edge b→c and the gate membership are gone. Removing the provider with `--force` exits 1.

evidence: spec/1.3.0.md §3 line 70-72: "a write whose after-state holds an error the before-state did not exits 1 naming the rule"; §4 line 85-86: "A cycle is one finding, `epic` its first member in file order, the message naming every member."; §9 row 2 (line 195) covers only a new rule slug (`cycle`) on a file holding `dangling-reference`.

If identity is the rule slug, a file that already has one `dangling-reference` accepts any number of new dangling edges, which defeats 'repaired one write at a time'. evidence: spec/1.3.0.md §4: "A cycle is one finding, `epic` its first member in file order, the message naming every member." §9 row 3 fixture: "a two-member cycle" (a single elementary cycle, the same under both readings).

A per-component implementation reports one `cycle` error and a per-elementary-cycle one reports two, so `errors` differs. Both follow the sentence. Row 3's 'two-member cycle' cannot tell them apart.
suggestion: Say one finding per strongly connected component (members in file order), and add an overlapping-cycle case to a §9 row.

evidence: spec/1.3.0.md §4 rows: "`no-dependencies` | warning | an epic outside the first milestone of its track has no dependencies"; "`thin-why` | warning | a non-empty `why` equals, or is wholly contained in, the target epic's id or title". §9 row 3 asserts on error slugs only; no row asserts `warnings`.

evidence: spec/1.3.0.md §5: "§4's error rules run over the whole file at every emission as `mechanical_checks` — a graph with a structural error is not reviewable in any slice". §9 row 11: "the file holds a cycle outside the slice and two clean rounds are recorded".

evidence: spec/1.3.0.md §5: 'From round 2, a unit whose hash is unchanged since the round before and that carried no open finding is marked `(carried)` and is not asked about again'; 'The built-in `regression` role is appended from round 2 when the slice changed since the round before or a finding was resolved `fixed`'. §9 row 7: 'round 2 is emitted over an unchanged slice and recorded with no rows … every unit `(carried)` in round 2'. Row 9: 'review_clean_rounds 2 … two rounds are recorded with no findings'.
finding: Once a slice records a clean round and is not edited, the next round is clean by construction, but it still costs a full panel emission. The carry marks a unit `(carried)` when its hash is unchanged and it has no open finding. After a clean round 1 on an unedited slice, every unit carries, and `regression` is not appended (nothing changed, nothing resolved `fixed`). Round 2 therefore asks no unit anything, yet it emits three role prompts and the agent spawns three reviewers to return empty files, only to reach `review_clean_rounds` 2. Row 7 pins exactly this round. That spends N subagent round-trips per converging slice, and the outcome is fixed before any of them runs.
suggestion: Derive the round. When every unit carries and no `regression` prompt is due, emission returns an empty `prompts[]`, and `next_action` says to record an empty file (or the record is implied). No reviewer is spawned for a round whose answer is already fixed.

evidence: Read spec/1.3.0.md §5: the hash covers 'its own block and the blocks of its direct dependencies'; the context is 'every epic one edge away in either direction'; `dod-satisfiability` asks 'that none of its dependencies, transitively, provides'. Round-1 finding #17 in review-round-1.ndjson, resolved fixed, quoted both halves.
finding: The repair of round-1 finding 'carry key is narrower than what dod-satisfiability asks' extends the hash to direct dependencies only, while the role still asks about the dependencies 'transitively' and the emission still shows only one hop. In the chain with slice `--epic a`, a `set` on `d`'s acceptance that removes a capability `a` relies on through `b` and `c` changes neither `a`'s block nor `b`'s, so `a` stays `(carried)` and is never asked again. The emission also never renders `c` or `d`, so the role cannot answer its transitive question for a fresh unit either. The finding's first half was fixed, its second half ('beyond one hop the dependencies are not even rendered') was not, and the role table was not narrowed to match.

evidence: spec/1.3.0.md §5: 'Each unit is rendered as a block: id, title, milestone, tags, acceptance, and each outgoing edge with its `why`'; 'The index lists every unit with a hash covering its own block and the blocks of its direct dependencies'; 'is marked `(carried)` and is not asked about again'; 'location is `epic:<id>` for a unit of the slice'. REFERENCE.md: ground rows join on the floor unit via text_sha/ordinal (engine/groundcarry.go groundJoinKey{textSHA, ordinal}).
finding: The spec does not say that a carried unit's block leaves the prompt. 'Is not asked about again' still allows the index line plus the full block (id, title, milestone, tags, acceptance, every edge with its why) for each carried unit, sent again to every role. On a mostly converged `--milestone` slice, nearly all of each prompt would then be text no reviewer is asked about. The per-unit hash in the index costs bytes for the same reason: in this loop rows are keyed by `location: epic:<id>`, not by hash, so the hash is tp's carry key, which tp stores and compares itself. No reviewer decision reads it. In `tp ground` the hash is part of the floor the rows join on, so reusing the index there does not carry the hash's purpose over to this loop.
suggestion: State that a carried unit appears only as its index line, and that its block is rendered only where it sits one edge from an asked unit (as context). Keep the hash in the state directory, not in the prompt index.

evidence: spec/1.3.0.md §5: "a `--milestone` slice adds one gate unit, the gate's members and deferrables" and "a hash covering its own block and the blocks of its direct dependencies" (a gate has no dependencies). §9: "'The chain' is `a → b → c → d`, all in milestone `A`", with no `gates`. Row 7: "every unit `(carried)` in round 2; in round 3 exactly `a` and … un-carried".

The §9 chain fixture defines no gates. Second, what does the gate unit's hash cover: member and deferrable ids only, or the members' blocks? 'Every unit (carried)' and 'exactly … un-carried' in row 7 depend on both answers. The second also decides whether editing a gate member's block re-asks the gate. Whether `gate:A` is a valid `--record` location in a `--milestone A` slice with no `gates.A` follows from the first.
suggestion: State that a milestone without a `gates` entry has no gate unit, or has an empty one, and that the gate unit's hash covers its member and deferrable id lists, or their blocks.

evidence: spec/1.3.0.md §5 line 121-122: "A graph role corpus, `.tp/epic-reviewers/`, ejected by `tp init --eject-roles` ... Every file in it is an active role, deleted to deactivate"; §7 line 166-168: Workflow E is "interview → `tp epic set milestones=…` → `tp epic add --bulk` → `tp epic lint` → `tp epic review` ..." with no eject; skills/tp/SKILL.md line 769: "The embedded default reviewers ... run `tp init --eject-roles` to read them" (embedded defaults are used without ejection).
finding: §5 defines the graph roles only as files in `.tp/epic-reviewers/` ('Every file in it is an active role'). It never says what `tp epic review` emits when that directory was never ejected. Workflow E (§7) has no eject step. `tp review` falls back to the embedded defaults when no corpus is ejected. A literal implementation of §5 emits zero role prompts in round 1 and no `regression` prompt, because that role is only added from round 2. An agent following Workflow E then records empty rounds and reaches `converged`/`--check` 0 without any role being asked, which defeats §1's goal. An implementation that falls back to the three embedded roles behaves differently.
suggestion: State that an absent `.tp/epic-reviewers/` means the three embedded graph roles, as `tp review` does, and that an ejected-then-emptied directory is refused rather than emitting zero prompts.

evidence: internal/cli/init.go line 148-168: `for _, phase := range []string{engine.PhaseReviewers, engine.PhaseAuditors}` … `if !initForce { if _, statErr := os.Stat(path); statErr == nil { output.Error(ExitFile, "role file already exists: …", "use --force to overwrite")`; skills/tp/REFERENCE.md line 704: "`tp init --eject-roles --force` | Overwrite existing role files regardless of validity"; spec/1.3.0.md §5 line 121: "`.tp/epic-reviewers/`, ejected by `tp init --eject-roles`".

A project that already ejected its reviewer/auditor corpus, tp's own repo included, either cannot obtain `.tp/epic-reviewers/` or must overwrite its customised reviewers to get it. Depending on phase order it may also be left with a partial eject. The spec does not say that eject changes, for example to skip existing files, eject per phase, or take an epic-only flag.
suggestion: Say how the graph corpus is ejected into a project that already has `.tp/reviewers/`: a separate flag or phase selector, or skipping phases whose directory already exists. Add a §9 row for it.

evidence: spec/1.3.0.md §5 line 135-137: "§4's error rules run over the whole file at every emission as `mechanical_checks` — a graph with a structural error is not reviewable in any slice" vs §9 row 11 (line 204): "the file holds a cycle outside the slice and two clean rounds are recorded | `mechanical_checks` names `cycle` as failing and `--status --check` exits 1".

Row 11 records two rounds over a graph holding a cycle, which assumes emission proceeds. The 'not reviewable' wording supports an implementation that refuses emission, and that implementation cannot build row 11's fixture. The two readings also put different first steps in Workflow E's loop.

evidence: spec/1.3.0.md §6: '`--json` writes the file's content as stored, normalised … `--compact` applies to `--json`'. spec/backlog/epics.md §8: '`tp epic export --json` writes the graph with every derived field filled'. spec/1.3.0.md §7 Workflow E lists set → add --bulk → lint → review, with no export step.
finding: In this release `tp epic export --json` is a copy of a tracked file the agent can already read at a known path. The decision record exists to fill derived fields ('writes the graph with every derived field filled'), and those fields ship in the second release; round 1's repair removed the last derived keys (`in_degree`, `out_degree`, `track`). What is left is 'the file's content as stored, normalised', a flag and a `--compact` mode that strips nothing defined, because stored content has no explanatory fields. No agent or renderer decision in this release needs it: Workflow E never calls it, and the write-deny fence blocks writes to `epics.json`, not reads.
suggestion: Ship `tp epic export --md` only in v1.3.0. Defer `--json` and its `--compact` to the second release, where derived fields give them content the stored file does not have.

evidence: Read spec/1.3.0.md §3 ('a write whose after-state holds an error the before-state did not exits 1') and §9 row 2. Traced the fixture: before {a: depends_on missing `b`} → add b(depends_on a): after-state has a cycle and no dangling edge, refused under both readings; the file is unchanged; then set a.depends_on=legal: after-state has no errors, so 'refuse any after-state error' also exits 0. Round-1 findings #9 and the 'reads two ways' finding asked for a row with a pre-existing error that separates Reading A from Reading B.
finding: Row 2 was rewritten to pin the round-1 decision (refuse only errors the before-state lacked) but cannot kill its own mutant. The fixture holds one error, a dangling edge on `a`. The `add` that closes `b → a → b` also removes that dangling error, so its after-state holds only `cycle` and both readings refuse it and name only `cycle`. The add writes nothing, so the following `set` that gives `a` a legal edge leaves a file with no error at all, and the mutant 'refuse any after-state error' exits 0 there too, not 1 as the row claims. The fixture also has only `a` in the file, so it names no target a legal edge could point at. Telling the two readings apart needs a file with two independent errors and a write that repairs one of them.

evidence: spec/1.3.0.md header: "reusing the spec loop's rules unchanged". skills/tp/SKILL.md:226-228: "Re-emitting an unrecorded round is idempotent while the spec is unchanged. A bare `tp ground <spec>` run twice returns the same `round` and rewrites the snapshot and floor byte-identically … `tp review` and `tp audit` follow the same rule." §9 row 18: "resolving the finding `wontfix` and re-emitting marks it".
finding: Row 18's second assertion re-emits round 2 after resolving a round-1 finding, with the graph unchanged, and expects the index to change (b now `(carried)`). §5 says the spec loop's rules are reused unchanged, and under that rule re-emitting an unrecorded round over an unchanged document returns the same round and rewrites the snapshot byte-identically. One correct implementation recomputes the carry on re-emission and passes. Another follows the inherited idempotence rule, keeps the round-2 snapshot byte-identical (b not carried), and fails.
suggestion: Either record round 2 and assert on round 3's index after the `wontfix`, or say in §5 that a disposition changes what re-emission computes, which carves an exception out of the idempotence rule.

evidence: spec/1.3.0.md §7 line 166-167: "`tp epic set milestones=…` on a new file"; §4 line 83: "3 when there is no file"; §9 row 20 (line 213): "an empty file; tracks `[[A]]`".
finding: No section says which writer creates `.tp/epics.json` when it is absent. Workflow E opens with `tp epic set milestones=…` 'on a new file', §4 gives lint exit 3 for a missing file, and row 20's fixture is 'an empty file', which is not valid JSON if it means zero bytes. An implementation that refuses `set` on a missing file and one that creates the file both satisfy §3 as written, but only the second runs Workflow E's first step.
suggestion: State that `tp epic set milestones=…` and `tp epic add` create the file with `version: 1` when it is absent, and make row 20's fixture 'no file'.

evidence: spec/1.3.0.md §3: '`tp epic set <top-level-field>=<json>` for `milestones`, `gates.<m>` and `tag_checks.<tag>`'. §4 `dangling-reference`: 'a gate member or deferrable … names no epic'. §7 Workflow E: 'tp epic set milestones=… on a new file → tp epic add --bulk'.
finding: `gates` and `tag_checks` can only be written one key per call (`gates.<m>`, `tag_checks.<tag>`), and each call re-lints the whole file. Seeding a graph with M gated milestones and T tag checks therefore takes M+T calls after `add --bulk`. A gate's members must already exist, or `dangling-reference` refuses the write, so these calls cannot come before the epics either. That breaks P2 for the file-level fields, though `--bulk` already fixed it for epics.
suggestion: Let the same `set` take the bare `gates=<json>` and `tag_checks=<json>` as whole objects, the form `milestones` already uses. Or point Workflow E's first topic at `tp epic import`, which writes the whole file in one call.

evidence: git -c diff.external= diff --no-ext-diff --no-index --word-diff=plain spec/.tp-review/1.3.0/snapshot-round-1.md spec/1.3.0.md, §5 'Roles' hunk: removed '[-default panel-] is [-three roles:-]', added 'Every file in it is an active role, deleted to deactivate, `domains` unread'.
finding: The repair of the activation-rules finding replaced 'following the same file schema and activation rules. The default panel is three roles' with 'Every file in it is an active role, deleted to deactivate'. That drops the statement that the three roles are the built-in default. It no longer says what `tp epic review` emits when `.tp/epic-reviewers/` is absent: the built-in three, the way the reviewer corpus falls back to built-ins, or no roles. The second case covers a project that ejected its reviewer corpus before 1.3.0, and any project that never ran `--eject-roles`.

evidence: spec/1.3.0.md §5: '`--status` carries `slice`, `round`, `consecutive_clean`, `converged`, `done`, `done_by`, `stale`, `carried`, `in_flight_round` and `next_action`'. REFERENCE.md:810: ground `--record` '`carried` the dispositions the carry brought forward'.
finding: Two of `--status`'s keys feed no decision this loop makes. `slice` echoes back the `--milestone`/`--epic` argument the agent just passed. `carried` is not defined: in `tp ground` it is the count of dispositions the carry wrote at record time, but this loop's carry writes no rows, and the emitted index already marks each carried unit. `consecutive_clean`, `converged`, `done`, `done_by`, `stale` and `next_action` already decide whether to run another round.
suggestion: Drop `slice` and `carried` from `--status`, or derive `carried` into `next_action`'s wording if a count is wanted.

evidence: spec/1.3.0.md §9 row 2 fixture: "a file with a dangling edge on `a`; first `add` closes a cycle `b → a → b`, then `set` replaces `a`'s `depends_on` with a legal edge"; §3: a refused write "writes nothing".
finding: Row 2's repairing step has no legal target. The fixture holds one epic `a` with a dangling edge. The `add` that would close `b → a → b` is refused and writes nothing, so `a` is still the only epic. "`set` replaces `a`'s `depends_on` with a legal edge" can then only point at `a` itself (a cycle) or at nothing. The row has to be read as `depends_on: []`, or the fixture needs a second epic.
suggestion: Add a second epic to the fixture as the legal target, or say "replaces `a`'s `depends_on` with `[]`".

evidence: spec/1.3.0.md §9 row 4: "removing the middle edge makes it fire on the dependent only"; fixture "`x → ui-rule-checker`, `screen` tagged `ui` with `screen → x`". §3: a write whose after-state adds an error "exits 1 … and writes nothing".
finding: Row 4's 'removing the middle edge' names no edge: `screen → x → ui-rule-checker` has two edges and no middle one. The removal also cannot go through a §3 writer, because it adds an `unprovided-tag-check` error and is refused. The test has to hand-edit the file, and the row does not say so.
suggestion: Name the edge (`x → ui-rule-checker`) and say that the second fixture is written directly, not through `tp epic set`.

evidence: spec/1.3.0.md §5: "refuses the whole file at exit 1, naming every offending line". §9 row 8: "exit 1 naming the line, write no round file" over "a three-row file whose second row's `location` is `epic:d` and third `gate:A`".
finding: Row 8 has two offending rows (`epic:d` and `gate:A`) but asserts 'naming the line', singular, while §5 requires naming every offending line. A record that stops at the first bad row and names only line 2 passes the row as written.
suggestion: Make row 8 assert that both lines 2 and 3 are named, and add 'name the first offending line only' as a mutant.
